::: {.apr}

Many engineering organizations are moving toward the same pattern: software approves small, low-risk pull requests, and people review the rest. We analyzed nine public write-ups of the pattern (eight from the organizations themselves, one relayed by a newsletter) and extracted 26 recurring themes. For each theme we counted how many of the sources mention it.

In the charts, each bar is a count of sources out of 9, drawn in two shades as keyed in the legend. "Substantial" means the source gives the theme a section, a specific mechanism or a number; "brief mention" means a sentence or a clear implication. The number in brackets is the substantial count. Hover a bar to see which sources.

Eight of the nine sources raise the same problem: AI-assisted engineers produce code faster than people can review it, and seven of them make that the main argument. The evidence is mostly throughput numbers. Meta reports significant lines per human-landed diff up 105.9% in a year and diffs per developer up 51%. At Assembled, median time to first review went from 3.5 hours (December 2025) to over 16 hours (May 2026). PostHog's monthly PR count went from 1,441 to 4,725 between January and June with headcount up about 10%. Ona's engineers open 10.8 PRs a week each, and Rewind counts about forty PRs a day competing for senior attention.

> Humans simply don’t have the time or mental capacity to properly review the volume of AI-generated code.
>
> — Intercom


Two further motives come up less often. Six sources argue that human review is itself imperfect, and that on routine changes it turns into rubber-stamping. Intercom notes that the product changes that caused its past outages "were all reviewed and approved by humans"; Rewind calls an unexamined approval "a rubber stamp wearing the costume of a control". Five sources point to the cost of waiting on the author: Customer.io opens on "the cognitive weight of waiting", and Ona describes authors deep in another task by the time approval arrives. Customer.io is the one source that does not describe a capacity bottleneck; its case rests on the author's wait.

Every source sorts changes by risk and gives the low-risk ones a lighter path. The tiers differ in form: Rewind grades every PR low, medium or high from what its reviewers found; Ona writes a six-criterion policy that must hold in full; Customer.io sorts changes into routine, structural and critical; Meta thresholds a risk score and requires its LLM reviewer to find every change in a safe category.

Eight of the nine also name changes that can never be auto-approved. This is what each post lists as ineligible. A filled cell means the post says so explicitly.

Size is the other common gate. Seven sources cap or measure diff size, and the numbers cluster: Ona and Assembled use under 1,000 lines; PostHog uses under 500 lines and 20 files. Customer.io measures lines, files and component boundaries but doesn't publish a cutoff. Intercom's agent refuses PRs it judges too big, complex or broad. Meta uses a review-effort score rather than lines.

One source disputes the proxy. Rewind argues diff size says little about risk, and sets a roughly 10,000-line ceiling only as a limit on human attention, "not as a risk signal".

> A twelve-line database migration that adds an index to a fifty-million-row table is one of the most dangerous things you can ship [...] A three-thousand-line PR that regenerates an API client from an updated schema is, in risk terms, nothing.
>
> — Rewind


PostHog's blog (read via a summary) treats line count as only a rough proxy for quality, while its newsletter piece describes the 500-line cap.

### How the review is done

The first chart in this part also shows how the review itself is built. Six sources use several narrowly scoped reviewers in place of one: Anthropic's review agents "do not share biases and blindspots", OpenAI uses domain specialists per infrastructure area, Intercom has sub-agents for intent, safety and logic, Assembled runs Codex and Claude Code independently, PostHog's qa-swarm spawns four reviewers, and Rewind convenes a "council" of a dozen or more.

Seven sources keep the final decision in deterministic code rather than in the model's judgment. Rewind sends findings to a unit-tested verdict engine ("The judgment is AI; the gate is not a vibe"). Assembled combines fixed rules, such as the 1,000-line cap, with LLM-based policies. PostHog's shared prompt says the LLM "can tighten gates but never loosen". In Meta's system any failed check routes the diff to a human.

### Where humans stay

"The AI approves PRs" covers three arrangements in these sources. Counts here are by source.

```{=html}
<div class="lanes"><div class="lane"><div class="lhead"><b>AI approves, human merges or ships</b><span class="lcount">5</span></div><p class="small">The bot clears the review requirement; a person still presses the button.</p><div class="chips"><span class="chip">Anthropic</span><span class="chip">OpenAI</span><span class="chip">PostHog</span><span class="chip">Rewind</span><span class="chip">Ona</span></div></div><div class="lane"><div class="lhead"><b>A slice lands with no human at all</b><span class="lcount">2</span></div><p class="small">For some class of change, nobody looks before it ships.</p><div class="chips"><span class="chip">Meta</span><span class="chip">Intercom</span></div></div><div class="lane"><div class="lhead"><b>Post doesn&#x27;t say</b><span class="lcount">2</span></div><p class="small">Approval is automated, but who merges isn&#x27;t stated.</p><div class="chips"><span class="chip">Customer.io</span><span class="chip">Assembled</span></div></div></div>
```


Ona and Rewind are the most explicit about why the human click matters. Ona: "a person always clicks the merge button", and that click is what its SOC 2 audit sees. Rewind: "Auto-approve is not auto-merge", and a PR authored by a bot "can never be merged without a human clicking the button". Both use the human merge as the answer to separation of duties.

Meta and Intercom go further for some changes. Meta lets bot-authored diffs that pass every gate land after a short delay in which a human can still reject them, and human-authored diffs that pass a stricter second step need no review at all, "not even deferred". Intercom says 497 PRs went "fully autonomous" in four weeks, "with Claude writing the code and our AI approval system reviewing, approving, and shipping to production".

Six sources keep an opt-in or override: Intercom says "any engineer can request a human review on any change, at any time", and in Rewind a `/request-jedi-review` comment stands the bot down. Four keep the reviewer independent of the author; PostHog's wording is that "the agent that wrote the code can’t be the one that reviews it".

The most common safeguards are about how the system is introduced and watched, not about the model. Six sources started in shadow mode or a pilot: Rewind spent its first week over 400+ repositories, with 90% agreement with human reviewers as the bar to go live, and Intercom piloted on 100+ PRs. Seven keep an audit trail of every AI verdict (Intercom: "Every AI-approved PR is labelled, logged, and queryable"), and seven run a loop where human reactions tune the policy, such as Intercom's helpful or not-helpful marks on review comments. Ona states the thesis directly: "The governance model matters more than the AI model."

Six address a compliance regime. Intercom engaged an auditor before scaling and maps to SOC 2, HIPAA and several ISO standards; Rewind brought its GRC lead in "at the start, not the end"; Ona treats the human merge click as the SOC 2 approval event. Meta excludes SOX-scoped code from automation.

Four put the approval rules themselves under change control. In Rewind the policy file is CODEOWNERS-protected and "the bot never edits its own prompts or policy". In Ona even swapping the model needs sign-off from the Head of Product Design and Engineering.

Six mention a production-side safety net, such as feature flags, rollback and monitoring, but only one (Intercom) discusses it at length. Intercom observes that most of its largest outages weren't caused by product-code changes at all.

The least-covered safeguard is the adversary. Only two sources (Anthropic and Rewind) consider a malicious or compromised author or agent. Anthropic describes an incident agent that, after a model upgrade, asked another agent to push a fix, and a human gate stopped it. Rewind lists "the bot approves a malicious PR" among thirteen failure modes in its risk assessment.

### Speed

Six sources report speed or throughput gains, and five give a latency number.

```{=html}
<div class="column-page"><div class="scroll"><table class="plain"><thead><tr><th>Who</th><th>Measure</th><th>Before</th><th>After</th><th>What it compares</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Ona</th><td>Median time to first approval</td><td class="nw">2h 49m</td><td class="nw">3.8 min</td><td class="small">Human-authored PRs; 4-week windows before and after; lead time also fell 74%.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Customer.io</th><td>Median merge time</td><td class="nw">3.5 hours</td><td class="nw">33 min</td><td class="small">AI-approved PRs vs the pre-system baseline; about 500 PRs over 3 months.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Intercom</th><td>Time to approval at p75</td><td class="nw">baseline</td><td class="nw">6 to 16x faster</td><td class="small">Controlled pilot of 100+ PRs.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Assembled</th><td>Median auto-review time</td><td class="nw">16h+ to first review (May)</td><td class="nw">8 min</td><td class="small">Different quantities: queue wait before, review duration after.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Meta</th><td>Median time to close</td><td class="nw">human-reviewed diffs</td><td class="nw">&#x27;over 330%&#x27; lower</td><td class="small">Difference-in-differences vs human-reviewed diffs; paper&#x27;s own phrasing.</td></tr></tbody></table></div></div>
```


No source reports a slowdown. Ona's is the clearest case: a step change on the day the bot approved its first PR, with a human still doing the merge, which Ona reads as evidence that "the approval wait was the real blocker".

### Safety

Seven sources report a revert, incident or bug number. This is every safety-flavoured number in the corpus, and what it actually covers.

approved diffs are the low-risk ones by construction (the paper says so under internal validity).</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Intercom</th><td>0 reverts in a 100+ PR pilot</td><td class="nw">Auto-approved PRs</td><td class="small">Small n; the 0.53% vs 5.39% revert figures cover all AI-authored code, not only approved PRs.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Rewind</th><td>0 reverts, 0 incidents; ~99% agreement with human reviewers</td><td class="nw">Auto-approved PRs</td><td class="small">One shadow week plus one live week; the post itself says 'directional'.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Assembled</th><td>Reverts steady at 0.8% per PR; bugs reported −27%</td><td class="nw">Whole org</td><td class="small">Three weeks; bugs lag, as the post says.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">PostHog</th><td>Revert share 0.2% (June 2026)</td><td class="nw">Whole monorepo</td><td class="small">Not split by approval path; read via a summary.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Anthropic</th><td>~⅓ of past claude.ai incident bugs would now be caught</td><td class="nw">Review system, retrospective</td><td class="small">Says nothing about approved-PR outcomes.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">OpenAI</th><td>~9 in 10 AI review comments flag valid issues</td><td class="nw">Review comments</td><td class="small">Precision of comments, not safety of approvals; relayed by Pragmatic Engineer.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Customer.io</th><td>No safety figure in the text</td><td class="nw">—</td><td class="small">Search snippets said 'zero incidents across 500 PRs'; not found on the page.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Ona</th><td>No safety figure</td><td class="nw">—</td><td class="small">Reports only speed and throughput.</td></tr></tbody></table></div></div>


Only three sources measure the PRs the system approved: Meta, Intercom (a pilot of about a hundred) and Rewind (about a week). Meta's own validity section is the most careful in the set: diffs are not randomly assigned, so a low revert rate on auto-approved diffs is partly built in, since those are the diffs chosen for being low-risk. Four sources say something about the limits of their own evidence: Meta, Assembled ("observational results from a rollout, not a randomized trial"), Rewind ("read them as directional") and Intercom.

Four report cost: Assembled about \$3.57 per review attempt, Rewind about \$0.73 per PR (over \$12 for large ones), PostHog about \$300 a month for StampHog, and Anthropic only that costs will rise with throughput. Three give a concrete case of the AI catching something a human might not. Intercom's agent flagged a one-line copy change that contradicted a validation elsewhere in the codebase, and Customer.io describes an embedded struct that would have leaked PII to an external service.

### Side effects on how people write PRs

Four sources report that the policy changed how engineers write PRs. Ona: large unfocused changes trip the criteria, so engineers "gravitate toward smaller, focused PRs". Intercom: refusing big PRs gives "a direct, positive incentive" to ship small ones. Assembled: to qualify, PRs started arriving with testing evidence and screenshots.

Three sources treat the same mechanism as a risk. Assembled: "our engineers ended up shaping PRs for the approval policy, so whatever the policy rewards, you get more of." Ona's answer is that engineers shouldn't classify their own changes, and automation "removes the temptation to game the system". Intercom takes up the worry about optimizing a ">50% AI-approved" metric and argues it isn't one.

Assembled reports two results nobody else does. A policy that is too strict fails quietly: engineers try it twice, get rejected and stop asking, so the time savings and the feedback both disappear. And throughput on large PRs, which the bot mostly doesn't approve, rose 3.5x. Their explanation is that reviewers no longer get buried in small PRs, so the ones that reach them get real attention.

### How far the evidence goes

- **Every source describes a system that is running.** None reports turning it off, and write-ups of abandoned systems wouldn't appear in a search like this one.
- **The windows are short.** Ona compares two four-week windows, Assembled has three weeks, Rewind has one live week. Bugs reported lag the PRs that cause them.
- **Three of the nine sell AI development tools** (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ona). That doesn't make them wrong, but they have a reason to report this well.
- **The sources are not fully independent.** Intercom is cited by both Anthropic and Rewind. Part of the "many companies" signal is a few companies reading each other.
- **Safe PRs are safe partly by selection.** Approved PRs were picked for being low-risk, so low revert rates on them are partly circular. Meta says this in its paper; most others don't.
- **Two sources are second-hand.** OpenAI is read through two Pragmatic Engineer articles. PostHog's 10,000-PR blog was read through a summary, so no quotes from it are used beyond what the newsletter piece supports.
- **Customer.io's "zero incidents across 500 PRs"** appeared in search snippets but not in the page text, so it isn't counted.
- **The coding is one reader's.** Two levels (substantial, brief), one coder. The note on every cell in the appendix gives the evidence so it can be checked.
- **Scope.** Vendor products that offer auto-approval (documentation, not experience reports) are not included.

```{=html}
<div id="tip" role="tooltip"></div><script>
(function(){
  var tip=document.getElementById('tip');
  function show(e,t){tip.textContent=t;tip.style.opacity=1;var x=e.clientX+14,y=e.clientY+14;
    var w=tip.offsetWidth,h=tip.offsetHeight;if(x+w>innerWidth-8)x=innerWidth-w-8;if(y+h>innerHeight-8)y=e.clientY-h-12;
    tip.style.left=x+'px';tip.style.top=y+'px';}
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-tip]').forEach(function(el){
    el.addEventListener('mousemove',function(e){show(e,el.dataset.tip)});
    el.addEventListener('mouseleave',function(){tip.style.opacity=0});
    el.addEventListener('focus',function(){var r=el.getBoundingClientRect();show({clientX:r.left,clientY:r.bottom},el.dataset.tip)});
    el.addEventListener('blur',function(){tip.style.opacity=0});
  });
  var sel=null;
  function fill(b){
    var d=b.closest('.viz').querySelector('.detail');
    if(sel)sel.classList.remove('sel');sel=b;b.classList.add('sel');d.classList.remove('empty');
    d.innerHTML='';var h=document.createElement('div');h.className='dh';h.textContent=b.dataset.s+' · '+b.dataset.t;
    var m=document.createElement('div');m.className='dm';m.textContent=b.dataset.l;
    var p=document.createElement('div');p.textContent=b.dataset.n;d.appendChild(h);d.appendChild(m);d.appendChild(p);}
  document.querySelectorAll('button.cell').forEach(function(b){
    b.addEventListener('click',function(){fill(b)});
    b.addEventListener('mouseenter',function(){fill(b)});
  });
})();
</script>
```
